summary:
Missions to the Moon’s south pole depend on sunlight for power and a clear line of sight to Earth for communication. Both are hard to get: the Sun and Earth sit only a few degrees above the horizon, terrain can hide them, and their cycles (about a year for the Sun, 27 days for Earth) rarely line up. Existing tools can calculate this, but their interfaces make quick comparison difficult.

Horizon Lens turns it into one readable screen:

Two-Sky View: the site’s terrain skyline with the Sun and Earth at true angular size, so you can see whether a ridge blocks them.
GO Ribbon: a timeline that is green when both are visible, amber when one is, and red when neither, so the best landing window stands out.
Compare Mode: up to four sites on the same dates, with scores for sunlit time, Earth-link time and longest outages.

Planner, Educator and Public modes serve mission planners, teachers and the public from one engine.

It follows NASA’s published landing requirements, includes NASA’s nine candidate Artemis regions as presets, and is designed around LRO terrain data and SPICE/JPL Horizons positions. As a validity check, we computed the Sun and Earth elevation at the lunar south pole for every hour of 2028. The results matched NASA’s published ranges (Sun about ±1.5°, Earth about ±6.8°).
details:
Horizon Lens is a single-screen Lunar Landing Site Navigator for the Moon’s south pole. It lets mission planners, educators and the public compare landing sites and dates by showing the Sun and Earth relative to the real terrain horizon.

How it works: For each site, we build a terrain skyline (a horizon mask across 360° of azimuth). We then combine it with Sun and Earth positions over time to test whether each body clears the skyline at each moment. The results appear in three views:

  • Two-Sky View: the skyline with the Sun (0.53°) and Earth (1.9°) drawn at true angular size.
  • GO Ribbon: a timeline that is green when Sun and Earth are both up, amber when one is, and red when neither is.
  • Compare Mode: up to four sites on the same dates, with scores for sunlit time, Earth-link time, longest dark spell and longest communication blackout.

Planner, Educator and Public modes serve different audiences from one engine.

Benefits and impact: It cuts the time to compare sites and dates from hours of expert tooling to seconds of looking. It supports power and direct-to-Earth communication planning for Artemis-era missions, and it makes the strange polar sky understandable to students and the public.

Tools: NASA’s Artemis Human Landing System requirements and the nine candidate Artemis regions guide the design. The architecture uses LRO/LOLA terrain data and SPICE/JPL Horizons positions. For our validation we used Python (Astropy, NumPy, Matplotlib), the IAU lunar rotation model, ReportLab for the brief, and Claude for drafting and code. [EDIT: list your actual app stack and hardware.]

Creativity: The GO Ribbon and true-scale Two-Sky View replace tables of angles with one glanceable strip.

Factors considered: We checked our computed 2028 pole results against NASA’s published figures. Sun elevation was about ±1.6° and Earth about ±6.8°, against NASA’s “~2° to 7°”. The smooth-sphere baseline has no terrain, so we state that limit openly. We also considered accessibility (patterns and labels as well as colour), shifting Artemis schedules, and antenna pointing limits.
